subject: biology
title: Protein structure and the proteome
summary: How amino acids fold into four levels of protein structure, why shape decides function, what the proteome is, and how cells make and export proteins through the secretory pathway.
body:
Proteins do almost every job in a cell: they speed up reactions, carry oxygen, signal between cells, fight infection and hold tissues together. What a protein can do depends entirely on its three-dimensional shape, and that shape comes from the order of its amino acids. In this lesson you will follow a protein from a chain of amino acids to a working molecule, and then follow it out of the cell.

## Key ideas

### Amino acids: the building blocks

Proteins are polymers made of **amino acids** (monomers). Every amino acid has the same backbone: a central carbon attached to an **amino group** (–NH₂), a **carboxyl group** (–COOH), a hydrogen atom and a variable side chain called the **R group**. There are 20 common amino acids, and they differ only in their R group. Some R groups are non-polar (hydrophobic), some are polar (hydrophilic), some carry a positive or negative charge, and one (cysteine) contains sulfur.

Amino acids join by a **condensation reaction** between the carboxyl group of one and the amino group of the next. A molecule of water is released and a **peptide bond** forms. A chain of many amino acids is a **polypeptide**. One end has a free amino group (the **N-terminus**) and the other a free carboxyl group (the **C-terminus**). A **protein** is one or more polypeptides folded into a functional shape.

### Primary structure

The **primary structure** is the sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, held together by peptide bonds (strong covalent bonds). The sequence is set by the gene that codes for the protein. Primary structure matters because it decides every higher level of folding: change one amino acid and the folding, and therefore the function, may change. Sickle-cell haemoglobin is a classic example, where a single amino acid substitution changes how the protein behaves.

### Secondary structure

**Secondary structure** is local folding of parts of the chain into regular shapes, held by **hydrogen bonds** between the backbone atoms (the C=O of one amino acid and the N–H of another, not the R groups). The two common forms are:

- **Alpha helix (α-helix)** — the chain coils into a spiral, with hydrogen bonds between amino acids about four positions apart.
- **Beta-pleated sheet (β-sheet)** — sections of chain lie side by side, folded like a zig-zag, with hydrogen bonds between neighbouring strands.

Some sections have no regular pattern and are called random coils or loops.

### Tertiary structure

**Tertiary structure** is the overall three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide. It forms from interactions between **R groups**, often far apart in the sequence:

- **Hydrophobic interactions** — non-polar R groups cluster in the middle, away from water.
- **Hydrogen bonds** between polar R groups.
- **Ionic bonds** between oppositely charged R groups.
- **Disulfide bridges** — strong covalent bonds between the sulfur atoms of two cysteines.

The tertiary structure creates the parts that do the work, such as an enzyme's **active site**. For a protein made of only one polypeptide, tertiary structure is its final, functional shape.

### Quaternary structure

**Quaternary structure** exists only when a protein is made of two or more polypeptide subunits. It is the way those subunits fit together, held by the same bonds as tertiary structure. Haemoglobin has four subunits (two α and two β chains), each holding an iron-containing haem group. Insulin is made of two polypeptides joined by disulfide bridges.

| Level | What it is | Main bonds |
|---|---|---|
| Primary | Amino acid sequence | Peptide (covalent) |
| Secondary | α-helices and β-sheets | Hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms |
| Tertiary | 3D shape of one polypeptide | R group interactions: hydrophobic, hydrogen, ionic, disulfide |
| Quaternary | Arrangement of several polypeptides | Same as tertiary, between subunits |

### Structure decides function

Because function depends on shape, anything that disrupts the weaker bonds can stop a protein working. **Denaturation** is a change to a protein's 3D shape (secondary, tertiary or quaternary) caused by things like high temperature or extreme pH. Heat makes the molecule vibrate until hydrogen and other weak bonds break; pH changes alter the charges on R groups and disrupt ionic and hydrogen bonds. The primary structure (peptide bonds) stays intact, but the active site or binding site loses its shape, so the protein no longer works.

Shape also suits each job: fibrous proteins such as collagen and keratin are long and strong for structure, while globular proteins such as enzymes, antibodies and haemoglobin are compact and soluble, with specific binding sites.

### The proteome

The **proteome** is the complete set of proteins expressed by a cell, tissue or organism at a given time under given conditions. It is different from the **genome** (all the DNA). Every cell in your body has essentially the same genome, but a liver cell and a muscle cell have very different proteomes because they express different genes. The proteome also changes over time, for example with age, diet, disease or stress. The proteome is larger than the number of genes because one gene can give rise to several proteins (for example through alternative splicing of mRNA) and proteins can be modified after translation. Studying the proteome (**proteomics**) helps scientists find disease markers and drug targets.

### The protein secretory pathway

Some proteins are made to leave the cell, such as digestive enzymes, antibodies and hormones like insulin. They travel through a series of organelles known as the **protein secretory pathway**:

1. **Rough endoplasmic reticulum (rough ER)** — ribosomes on its surface translate mRNA, and the growing polypeptide is fed into the ER's internal space (lumen), where it begins to fold.
2. **Transport vesicle** — the protein is packaged into a small membrane sac that buds off the rough ER and travels to the Golgi apparatus.
3. **Golgi apparatus** — the vesicle fuses with the Golgi, which modifies the protein (for example by adding carbohydrate groups), sorts it and packages it into new vesicles.
4. **Secretory vesicle** — buds off the Golgi and moves to the plasma membrane.
5. **Exocytosis** — the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane and releases the protein outside the cell.

Proteins used inside the cytosol are usually made on free ribosomes and do not go through this pathway.

## Worked examples

### Example 1: Explaining loss of function

*An enzyme from a human stomach works well at pH 2 but stops working at pH 8. Explain why.*

1. Identify the level affected: pH changes the charges on R groups.
2. Link to bonds: changing charge disrupts ionic bonds and hydrogen bonds between R groups, which hold the tertiary structure.
3. Link to shape: the tertiary structure changes, so the active site changes shape.
4. Link to function: the substrate no longer fits the active site, so the enzyme cannot catalyse the reaction. The enzyme has been denatured; its primary structure is unchanged.

### Example 2: Tracking a radioactive label

*Pancreatic cells were given amino acids labelled with a radioactive marker. Researchers recorded where most of the label was found over time.*

| Time (minutes) | Location of most label |
|---|---|
| 5 | Rough ER |
| 20 | Golgi apparatus |
| 40 | Vesicles near the plasma membrane |
| 90 | Outside the cell |

1. The labelled amino acids are built into new proteins on ribosomes attached to the rough ER, so the label appears there first.
2. Transport vesicles carry the protein to the Golgi, where it is modified and packaged.
3. Secretory vesicles move to the plasma membrane.
4. Exocytosis releases the protein, so the label ends up outside the cell. The order of results matches the secretory pathway, so the protein is a secreted protein (such as a digestive enzyme or insulin).

## Common mistakes

- Saying denaturation breaks peptide bonds. It does not; it disrupts the weaker bonds holding secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure.
- Saying secondary structure comes from R group interactions. Secondary structure comes from hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms; tertiary comes from R groups.
- Saying every protein has quaternary structure. Only proteins with two or more polypeptides do.
- Mixing up the proteome and the genome. Cells share a genome but differ in proteome.
- Leaving out vesicles in the secretory pathway, or saying the Golgi makes proteins. Ribosomes make them; the Golgi modifies and packages them.

## Exam tips

- In 'explain' questions, chain your answer: change in condition → bonds disrupted → shape changes → active or binding site no longer fits → function lost.
- Name the bonds for each level precisely; vague answers like 'bonds break' rarely earn full marks.
- For the secretory pathway, name each organelle and say what it does, in the correct order, finishing with exocytosis.
- Be ready to interpret diagrams of protein structure or tables of data like the radioactive label example.

## Key terms

- **Amino acid** — monomer of proteins with an amino group, carboxyl group, hydrogen and R group.
- **Peptide bond** — covalent bond joining two amino acids, formed by condensation.
- **Polypeptide** — a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds.
- **Primary structure** — the sequence of amino acids.
- **Secondary structure** — α-helices and β-pleated sheets held by backbone hydrogen bonds.
- **Tertiary structure** — 3D shape of one polypeptide from R group interactions.
- **Quaternary structure** — arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits.
- **Disulfide bridge** — covalent bond between sulfur atoms of two cysteine R groups.
- **Denaturation** — loss of a protein's 3D shape and function due to heat, pH or other factors.
- **Proteome** — all the proteins expressed by a cell, tissue or organism at a given time.
- **Exocytosis** — release of materials from a cell when a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane.

## Summary

- Proteins are polymers of amino acids joined by peptide bonds in condensation reactions.
- Primary structure is the sequence; secondary structure is α-helices and β-sheets held by backbone hydrogen bonds.
- Tertiary structure is the 3D shape from R group interactions; quaternary structure is the joining of several polypeptides.
- A protein's shape determines its function; denaturation changes shape and stops function without breaking peptide bonds.
- The proteome is all proteins expressed at a given time and varies between cell types and over time.
- Secreted proteins travel rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi → secretory vesicle → exocytosis.

questions.prompt: Which bonds are mainly responsible for holding the secondary structure of a protein?

options.A: Peptide bonds between adjacent amino acids
options.B: Hydrogen bonds between atoms of the polypeptide backbone
options.C: Ionic bonds between charged R groups
options.D: Disulfide bridges between cysteine R groups

questions.explanation: α-helices and β-sheets are held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H groups of the backbone. Ionic bonds between R groups are tempting, but R group interactions build tertiary structure, not secondary structure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines the proteome?

options.A: All the genes in an organism's DNA
options.B: All the amino acids available inside a cell
options.C: The complete set of proteins an organism could ever produce, which is the same in every cell
options.D: The complete set of proteins expressed by a cell, tissue or organism at a given time

questions.explanation: The proteome is the full set of proteins actually expressed at a given time and under given conditions. Option C is tempting, but the proteome differs between cell types and changes over time, unlike the genome.

questions.prompt: A protein is heated to 70 °C and loses its function. Which level of structure remains unchanged?
questions.explanation: Heat disrupts weak bonds such as hydrogen and ionic bonds, changing secondary, tertiary and quaternary structure. Peptide bonds are strong covalent bonds and are not broken, so the amino acid sequence remains. Option D is tempting but wrong because denaturation does not break the chain apart.

questions.prompt: Which statement about quaternary structure is correct?

options.A: All functional proteins have quaternary structure.
options.B: Quaternary structure is formed by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms only.
options.C: Quaternary structure is only present in proteins made of two or more polypeptide chains.
options.D: Quaternary structure refers to the sequence of amino acids in each subunit.

questions.explanation: Quaternary structure is the arrangement of two or more polypeptide subunits, as in haemoglobin. Option A is a common misconception: many proteins are a single polypeptide and their final shape is their tertiary structure.

questions.prompt: A muscle cell and a skin cell from the same person contain the same genome. Why do they have different proteomes?

options.A: Each cell type contains different genes.
options.B: Muscle cells have more ribosomes, so they translate every gene faster.
options.C: Different genes are expressed in each cell type, so different proteins are made.
options.D: Skin cells lose some of their chromosomes as they mature.

questions.explanation: Both cells carry the same DNA but switch on different sets of genes, producing different proteins. Option A is tempting, but body cells of one person share essentially the same genome; the difference is in gene expression.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes the pathway of a protein that is secreted from a cell?

options.A: Ribosome on rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → exocytosis
options.B: Free ribosome in cytosol → Golgi apparatus → rough ER → exocytosis
options.C: Golgi apparatus → rough ER → transport vesicle → exocytosis
options.D: Ribosome on rough ER → Golgi apparatus → nucleus → secretory vesicle → exocytosis

questions.explanation: Secreted proteins are made on ribosomes on the rough ER, carried by a vesicle to the Golgi for modification and packaging, then moved in a secretory vesicle to the plasma membrane and released by exocytosis. Option C reverses the order of the rough ER and Golgi, a common error.

questions.prompt: In an enzyme, a cysteine at position 45 forms a disulfide bridge with a cysteine at position 210. A mutation replaces cysteine 45 with a different amino acid. What is the most likely effect?

options.A: Only the secondary structure changes, so the enzyme works normally.
options.B: The enzyme gains a second active site.
options.C: The peptide bonds either side of position 45 break.
options.D: The tertiary structure may change, altering the active site and reducing activity.

questions.explanation: Disulfide bridges help hold the tertiary structure. Losing one can change the 3D shape, including the active site, so the substrate may no longer fit. Option A is tempting, but a change in primary structure affects R group interactions, which govern tertiary structure.

questions.prompt: A scientist adds a drug that stops vesicles fusing with the plasma membrane in pancreatic cells that make insulin. Where would insulin most likely build up?

options.B: In secretory vesicles inside the cell
options.C: In the blood outside the cell
options.D: On free ribosomes in the cytosol

questions.explanation: If vesicles cannot fuse with the plasma membrane, exocytosis is blocked, so insulin stays packaged in secretory vesicles. Option C is wrong because insulin cannot leave the cell without exocytosis; option D is wrong because insulin is made on ribosomes attached to the rough ER.
